6Theory: state size is recall capacity

The most important result in the field, and the reason pure linear models have not replaced transformers.

Theorem (Arora et al., informal)

Any recurrent model depending causally on its input requires Ω(N) bits of state to solve multi-query associative recall over NNN items. The trade-off is information-theoretic, not architectural — no cleverness in the update rule escapes it. A fixed-size state can only hold a fixed amount, and recall demands grow with context length.

Reading the notation: Ω(N)\Omega (N)Ω(N) is a lower bound — "at least on the order of NNN" — as opposed to O(N)O(N)O(N), which is an upper bound. And information-theoretic means the limit follows from counting bits, not from any property of transformers or SSMs: you cannot store NNN independent facts in fewer than ∼N\sim N∼N bits, whatever architecture you wrap around them. See Appendix B.

What this does and does not say, carefully:

  • It does say: for any fixed state size there is a context length beyond which exact recall fails. A fixed-state model cannot guarantee every arbitrary long-context lookup, but it can preserve selected facts at long distances; the lower bound is worst-case rather than a claim that every API-key query fails.
  • It does not say linear models are bad. Most tokens don't need recall — and the constant matters enormously. Better write rules (delta over accumulation, channel-wise over scalar gates) move you up the frontier at the same state size, which is exactly what §3–§4 achieve.
  • It explains the hybrids in §7: if you need unbounded recall on some queries, keep a few layers that have unbounded state and let the rest be linear.

There is a second, complementary line of theory worth knowing: linear attention (and SSMs) are streaming models — they see each token once, in order, and may keep only a bounded summary — so they fall in a small-space complexity class (complexity measured in memory used rather than time taken). They can be shown unable to solve problems requiring more than constant memory per token, which is the same fact as the theorem above viewed through complexity theory rather than information theory.

Derivation: prove a finite-state recall lower bound by counting

A precise task. There are N known distinct keys; each is assigned an independent value from an alphabet of size V. After reading all N assignments, a deterministic recurrent model must answer a query for any one key with zero error. It retains at most b bits of state and no external copy of the assignments. The query is chosen after encoding.

  1. There are VN possible assignment tables.
  2. A b-bit state can take at most 2b values.
  3. If 2b<VN, the pigeonhole principle gives two distinct tables with the same state.
  4. The tables differ at some key. Querying that key supplies the same query and state to the decoder, but requires different answers. At least one answer must be wrong.
Zero-error recall for every assignment:2b≥VNb≥Nlog⁡2V bits\begin{aligned}\text{Zero-error recall for every assignment:}\quad2^b&\ge V^N\\ b&\ge N\log_2V\ \mathrm{bits}\end{aligned}Zero-error recall for every assignment:2bb​≥VN≥Nlog2​V bits​

For 1,000 arbitrary byte-valued facts, this toy task requires at least 8,000 retained bits, before key encoding or implementation overhead. A fixed floating-point state has a finite bit budget, so unlimited recurrence does not defeat this bound. Infinite-precision real numbers would invalidate the finite-state counting premise, which is why precision must be stated.

This proof is a worst-case zero-error result. It does not say that every fact at a long distance is forgotten, that a specially marked API key cannot be preserved, or that an ordinary transformer always retrieves correctly. Restricted data distributions, lossy answers, probabilistic error, compression of redundant facts, and external memory change the task. The BASED paper’s MQAR analysis formalizes a related recall–state tradeoff; this elementary version explains the essential information bottleneck without importing all of that theorem’s details.

Exercise — Separate a worst-case guarantee from a useful heuristic

A recurrent state has 4,096 bits. Can it guarantee zero-error recall of every one of 600 independent byte-valued facts? Could it still always retain one designated 32-byte API key? Explain both using the counting bound.

Show worked solution

The 600-fact task needs at least 600·8=4,800 bits, exceeding 4,096, so no such worst-case guarantee is possible under the stated assumptions. One designated 32-byte key contains only 256 bits, so the counting argument does not forbid retaining it exactly, even after a long stream. It does not prove the trained model learns to do so; it only removes the claimed information-theoretic impossibility for that restricted task.

7Hybrids: what actually ships

Problems defining this stage. Finite recurrent state cannot retain arbitrarily many exact associations. Hybrid architectures allocate some layers to explicit attention and others to compressed recurrent memory, trading cache growth against retrieval precision and the cost of state updates.

No frontier model is purely linear. Every one of them is a mixture, and the interesting question is the ratio.

ModelMixRatio and notes
Jamba

Core idea. Interleave Mamba, attention and MoE components so recurrent layers reduce sequence-state cost while attention layers retain explicit token interactions.

(2024)		Mamba + attention + MoE1 attention layer per 8 (1:7), MoE every 2 layers. The first production-grade hybrid. In ablations the hybrid beat both pure Transformer and pure Mamba throughout training — the mixture is better than either parent, not just cheaper.
Samba

Core idea. Combine Mamba with sliding-window attention: recurrence carries compressed long-range information while local attention preserves more precise nearby interactions.

(2025)		Mamba + sliding-window attentionWindow 2048. Extrapolates to 256K with minimal fine-tuning: the window handles local precision, the recurrent state handles long-range gist.
MiniMax-01

Core idea. Use mostly Lightning Attention layers with occasional full attention, limiting how often the model pays for an explicit global token cache.

(2025)		Lightning Attention + full attention7:1. The aggressive end — 1M+ token context, at some cost in precise retrieval. Demonstrated that linear attention scales to 456B parameters.
Qwen3-Next

Core idea. Mix Gated DeltaNet with gated attention, using targeted recurrent updates for most layers while retaining explicit attention in a smaller fraction.

(2025)		Gated DeltaNet + gated attention3:1. Their finding: 25% softmax layers suffice to preserve needle-in-a-haystack, long CoT and tool use, while 75% linear layers cut the cost. Reported as the best price/performance point.
Kimi Linear

Core idea. Pair channel-wise KDA recurrent updates with gated MLA layers, improving both the compressed-memory path and its attention complement.

(2025)		KDA + gated MLA≈3:1, with both layer types upgraded — KDA moves the decay from a scalar per head to a value per channel.
Why hybrids work, stated plainly

The theorem in §6 says a bounded state cannot do unbounded recall. It says nothing about needing every layer to do unbounded recall. A single full-attention layer gives the residual stream access to any position; the linear layers then do the bulk of the processing cheaply. Empirically the crossover is around 1 in 4 — below that, retrieval degrades; above it, you are paying for attention you don't need. That 3:1–7:1 band is the most reproducible number in this guide.

Sliding-window attention as the third ingredient. Several designs (Samba, Gated DeltaNet-H1, GPT-OSS, Gemma 3) use SWA rather than full attention as the "precise" component, because a fixed window is also O(1)O(1)O(1) state per token — a window of 128–2048 tokens adds negligible KV cache. You then have three tiers: recurrent state for the gist, a window for local precision, and occasional full attention for genuine retrieval.

Derivation: derive the hybrid memory curve and what a full-attention layer changes

Homogeneous layer accounting. Suppose L layers share the same widths, fraction f use full KV attention, and the rest use a fixed state of s bytes per layer and sequence. Let c=2Hkvdbkv be full-attention KV bytes per context token per layer. Then:

Mhybrid(n)=L[fcn+(1−f)s]MhybridMdense=f+(1−f)scnlim⁡n→∞MhybridMdense=f(f>0)\begin{aligned}M_{\mathrm{hybrid}}(n)&=L[fcn+(1-f)s]\\ \frac{M_{\mathrm{hybrid}}}{M_{\mathrm{dense}}}&=f+(1-f)\frac{s}{cn}\\ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_{\mathrm{hybrid}}}{M_{\mathrm{dense}}}&=f\quad(f>0)\end{aligned}Mhybrid​(n)Mdense​Mhybrid​​n→∞lim​Mdense​Mhybrid​​​=L[fcn+(1−f)s]=f+(1−f)cns​=f(f>0)​

A 3:1 linear/full-attention mixture has f=1/4, so its asymptotic KV-memory improvement is at most 4× under matched widths and cache precision, even if linear-layer state is negligible. The hundreds-fold state comparison of a single linear layer must not be applied to the entire hybrid. A 7:1 mixture tends to 8×. For window layers, replace n by min(n,w); if every attention layer is windowed, total stored state is bounded in n and the unrestricted recall counting limit still applies to the complete architecture.

A full-attention layer creates access to all stored positions at that layer. It does not prove that one such layer suffices for every task or that 25% is a universal optimum. Depth, width, representations, training data, and where the attention layers are placed affect the ability to compose several retrieved facts. Report empirical hybrid-ratio sweeps as empirical, while using this equation for their storage consequence.

8Hardware

The section that motivates the whole enterprise: what linear attention does to the memory system.

8.1 The decode arithmetic — why this is a bandwidth story

Softmax:F≈4ndh,M≈2ndhp,I≈2/pLinear:F≈4dkdv,M≈2dkdvp,I≈2/pState read and write in HBM; other operations add traffic.n=131072, dh=128, p=2, Hkv=8, L=64MKV=2⋅131072⋅8⋅128⋅64⋅2≈34 GBMstate=128⋅128⋅32⋅64⋅2≈67 MBBoth memory bound; the linear state is about 500× smaller.\begin{aligned}\text{Softmax:}\quad F&\approx4nd_h,\quad M\approx2nd_hp,\quad I\approx2/p\\ \text{Linear:}\quad F&\approx4d_kd_v,\quad M\approx2d_kd_vp,\quad I\approx2/p\\ &\text{State read and write in HBM; other operations add traffic.}\\ n&=131072,\ d_h=128,\ p=2,\ H_{\mathrm{kv}}=8,\ L=64\\ M_{\mathrm{KV}}&=2\cdot131072\cdot8\cdot128\cdot64\cdot2\approx34\ \mathrm{GB}\\ M_{\mathrm{state}}&=128\cdot128\cdot32\cdot64\cdot2\approx67\ \mathrm{MB}\\ &\text{Both memory bound; the linear state is about }500\times\text{ smaller.}\end{aligned}Softmax:FLinear:FnMKV​Mstate​​≈4ndh​,M≈2ndh​p,I≈2/p≈4dk​dv​,M≈2dk​dv​p,I≈2/pState read and write in HBM; other operations add traffic.=131072, dh​=128, p=2, Hkv​=8, L=64=2⋅131072⋅8⋅128⋅64⋅2≈34 GB=128⋅128⋅32⋅64⋅2≈67 MBBoth memory bound; the linear state is about 500× smaller.​
The three consequences for a serving system
  1. Decode cost is independent of position. Token 1 and token 1,000,000 cost the same. The cost curve flattens completely — compare the DeepSeek DSA cost curves in the sparse-attention guide, which only bend.
  2. Batch size stops being limited by the KV cache. This is the largest practical effect. The state is per-sequence and tiny, so you can hold far more concurrent sequences in HBM, which raises the weight-loading amortisation across the batch — a second-order win that is often bigger than the first-order one.
  3. Latency becomes insensitive to batch size. RetNet observed exactly this. When the per-sequence state is tiny, adding sequences adds arithmetic against weights you were loading anyway.

The flip side, which papers rarely state: at small nnn, linear attention reads a d×dd\times dd×d state where softmax attention would read a tiny cache, and d2d^{2}d2 can exceed n⋅dn\cdot dn⋅d. Below the crossover (≈2K tokens) you are strictly worse off (§1.3).

Derivation: derive recurrent-state traffic and an accumulation-error budget

One additive matrix state. For the ungated update S←S+kvᵀ, each state cell requires one product and one addition, approximately 2mdv FLOPs. The readout qᵀS costs another 2mdv, totaling approximately 4mdv. A scalar-gated update S←aS+kvᵀ with nontrivial a adds one multiplication per state cell: approximately 5mdv including readout. Fusion can reduce instructions or intermediate traffic; it does not erase the gate multiplication from the FLOP count. If the persistent state lives in HBM between decode steps, the update must both read and write mdv scalars. Thus state-only traffic is approximately 2mdvbs.

Iungated≈4mdv2mdvbs=2bsIscalar-gated≈5mdv2mdvbs=2.5bsbs=4:I≈0.5 or 0.625 FLOP/byteMamortized/token≈2mdvbsCif resident across C tokens\begin{aligned}I_{\mathrm{ungated}}&\approx\frac{4md_v}{2md_vb_s}=\frac2{b_s}\\ I_{\mathrm{scalar\text{-}gated}}&\approx\frac{5md_v}{2md_vb_s}=\frac{2.5}{b_s}\\ b_s=4:&\quad I\approx0.5\text{ or }0.625\ \mathrm{FLOP/byte}\\ M_{\mathrm{amortized/token}}&\approx\frac{2md_vb_s}{C}\quad\text{if resident across }C\text{ tokens}\end{aligned}Iungated​Iscalar-gated​bs​=4:Mamortized/token​​≈2mdv​bs​4mdv​​=bs​2​≈2mdv​bs​5mdv​​=bs​2.5​I≈0.5 or 0.625 FLOP/byte≈C2mdv​bs​​if resident across C tokens​

For floating-point accumulation, a classical bound for summing n terms is ∣fl⁡(∑ixi)−∑ixi∣≤γn∑i∣xi∣|\operatorname{fl}(\sum_ix_i)-\sum_ix_i|\le\gamma_n\sum_i|x_i|∣fl(∑i​xi​)−∑i​xi​∣≤γn​∑i​∣xi​∣, where γn=nu1−nu\gamma_n=\frac{nu}{1-nu}γn​=1−nunu​ when nu<1 and u is unit roundoff. This is an absolute-error bound; cancellation can make relative error much larger. BF16 has u≈2⁻⁸, so this worst-case bound stops being informative around n=256. FP32 has u≈2⁻²⁴ and remains informative far longer. Fused accumulation, pairwise reductions, rescaling, and decay can improve actual behavior; the bound is a diagnostic, not a prediction of inevitable failure.

With a contractive scalar gate |a|≤ρ<1 and at most ε absolute error injected per step, recurrence gives ∥et∥≤ρ∥et−1∥+ε\|e_t\|\le \rho \|e_{t-1}\|+\varepsilon ∥et​∥≤ρ∥et−1​∥+ε. Unrolling from e₀=0 yields ∥et∥≤ε(1−ρt)1−ρ\|e_t\|\le\frac{\varepsilon(1-\rho^t)}{1-\rho}∥et​∥≤1−ρε(1−ρt)​. Forgetting limits accumulated numerical error, but also erases old content. This is a concrete accuracy–memory-horizon trade rather than a rule that one precision is always sufficient.

Exercise — Use a contraction bound to size a numerical tolerance

A recurrence contracts old error by at most ρ=0.99 each step and injects at most 10⁻⁵ new error per step. Bound the error after 100 steps and as t→∞. What changes if ρ=1?

Show worked solution

At 100 steps, the bound is 10⁻⁵(1−0.99¹⁰⁰)/0.01≈0.000633968. Its infinite-horizon limit is 10⁻⁵/0.01=0.001. If ρ=1, unrolling gives at most t·10⁻⁵, so there is no time-independent bound of this form. This analysis assumes a uniform contraction and a uniform additive error bound; a data-dependent nonlinear block needs those assumptions checked or replaced.

8.2 Tensor cores and precision

  • Keep everything in matmul form. The single biggest lever, and the reason SSD beat Mamba's hand-written scan by 2–8×. A bespoke sequential scan uses a fraction of a modern GPU's peak; a matmul uses all of it. When evaluating a proposed recurrence, the first question is "does its chunk update reduce to GEMM?"
  • Precision is not uniform. The state accumulator generally wants FP32 — it is a running sum over thousands of outer products and BF16 accumulation drifts. The QK⊤QK^\top QK⊤ and K⊤VK^\top VK⊤V matmuls can be BF16/FP8. The gate computation, if in log space, must be FP32 and cannot use tensor cores, which is the constraint driving GLA's secondary chunking (§3).
  • Chunk size is a memory-hierarchy parameter, not a modelling one. Choose CCC so that C×CC\times CC×C scores plus C×dC\times dC×d of K,VK, VK,V plus the d×dd\times dd×d state fit in SRAM simultaneously. On an H100 (228 KB shared memory per SM) with dhd_hdh​ = 64–128 this lands at CCC = 64–128. That is why every paper uses those numbers.
  • State size is a real memory-hierarchy decision. dk×dvd_k \times d_vdk​×dv​ per head, per layer. A larger state improves recall (§6) but must stay resident; once it spills out of SRAM into HBM every token, you have reinvented the KV cache with worse constants.

8.3 A checklist for silicon

If you are designing an accelerator and want linear-attention and hybrid models to run well on it:

  • SRAM sized for state + chunk tile. The working set is dk⋅dvd_k\cdot d_vdk​⋅dv​ (state) + C⋅dC\cdot dC⋅d (K, V, Q tiles) + C2C^{2}C2 (scores) per head in flight. Getting this resident is the entire optimisation. Concretely: with ddd = 128 and CCC = 128 in BF16 that is ~32 KB + ~96 KB + ~32 KB per head.
  • FP32 accumulation paths with BF16/FP8 inputs. Standard for GEMM, but note the accumulator here is persistent across the chunk loop, not per-tile — it must survive in registers or SRAM, not be flushed.
  • Cheap elementwise-and-exp units near the accumulator. Gates need sigmoid/exp/cumulative products per channel between matmuls. If these round-trip to HBM you lose the benefit; a fused elementwise unit adjacent to the tensor unit is worth real area.
  • Efficient small-matrix GEMM. The d×dd\times dd×d state update is a small matmul. Systolic arrays sized for 256×256 tiles idle on a 128×128 update; support for small-tile GEMM at high utilisation matters more here than peak TFLOPS.
  • Plan for heterogeneity. Hybrid stacks combine recurrent state with context-growing attention KV. Recurrent prefill and training can be compute intensive after chunking, whereas recurrent decode can be state-traffic limited. Full-attention costs change with context and GQA. Provision and benchmark both kernel families at the intended batch, phase, and precision.
  • Don't over-index on a fixed ddd. Head dimensions, state dimensions and expansion factors vary across models, and state size is the knob designers use to buy recall. Parameterise.

9Decision guide

SituationRecommendation
Context < 4KBenchmark before changing architecture: optimized softmax attention may be faster below the implementation-specific crossover. It retains full KV representations, but learned retrieval is not guaranteed lossless.
Very long context, gist-style tasks (summarisation, long-form generation)Aggressive hybrid, 7:1. MiniMax-01's regime.
Long context with retrieval (RAG, agents, code over large repos)Conservative hybrid, 3:1, with Gated DeltaNet or KDA as the linear layer. Qwen3-Next's regime, and the safer default.
KV-cache memory is the binding constraintHybrid. This is where linear attention pays off most and the effect (≈500× smaller state) dwarfs anything quantization or sparsity gives you.
Edge / on-device, no HBMStrongly favours linear. Constant state fits in SRAM; unbounded KV does not.
Building the linear layer from scratchGated DeltaNet (decay + delta rule) with a chunkwise WY kernel. It is the current best trade-off and has open implementations.
Converting an existing transformerDistillation into a hybrid, keeping ~25% of attention layers. Initialisation matters a lot — this is an active research area, not a solved recipe.
Designing siliconAssume hybrids. Size SRAM for state + chunk tile; support small-tile GEMM; fuse the elementwise gate path. §8.3.

10Open problems

  1. Moving up the Pareto frontier, not along it. The delta rule was one genuine jump. Momentum, higher-order updates and channel-wise erase/write gates are incremental. What would a qualitatively better write rule look like? The "state as online learner" framing (§4) suggests the answer is a better optimiser, but nobody has demonstrated a decisive one.
  2. Escaping the bound with structure rather than size. 2026 work explores sparse states and auxiliary exact memories for "what the recurrent state forgets." If a small exact side-memory can be maintained cheaply, the hybrid ratio could drop further.
  3. The right hybrid ratio, derived rather than swept. 3:1 and 7:1 are empirical. Nobody can predict the ratio from a task distribution, and nobody knows whether the optimum shifts with scale.
  4. Distilling attention into linear layers. Converting a trained transformer cheaply would change the economics overnight. Current methods need substantial continued training and the initialisation problem is not solved.
  5. Long-context RL and test-time compute. Long reasoning chains are exactly the regime where linear attention should win on cost — and exactly the regime where losing recall over one's own chain of thought is most dangerous. Largely unstudied.
  6. Kernels for heterogeneous stacks. Serving a 3:1 hybrid efficiently means alternating between two very different kernels with different memory behaviour, plus two different cache structures in the same request. The systems work here lags the modelling work badly.
  7. Numerics at scale. FP32 accumulators, log-space gates and 1M-token sequences interact in ways that are under-documented; most stability tricks in this literature are folklore.

11Reading list

  1. start hereKatharopoulos, Vyas, Pappas & Fleuret — Transformers are RNNs (ICML 2020). arXiv:2006.16236. The associativity trick and the RNN duality, in the clearest form anyone has written it. §3 is four pages and is the foundation of everything here.
  2. start hereYang, Wang, Shen, Panda & Kim — Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training (ICML 2024). arXiv:2312.06635. The chunkwise form, FlashLinearAttention, secondary chunking, and an unusually honest account of what tensor cores will and won't do. The single most useful paper for a hardware reader.
  3. Sun et al. — Retentive Network (RetNet) (2023). arXiv:2307.08621. Read Fig. 4 — the three computation paradigms side by side in twenty lines of pseudocode each.
  4. Dao & Gu — Transformers are SSMs (SSD / Mamba-2) (ICML 2024). arXiv:2405.21060. The duality, and the lesson that reformulating a scan as matmuls is worth 2–8×. Long; §§3–6 are the core.
  5. Arora et al. — BASED: Simple linear attention LMs balance the recall–throughput tradeoff (ICML 2024). arXiv:2402.18668. The state-size/recall frontier and the Ω(N)-bits theorem. Read this before believing any "matches transformer quality" claim.
  6. Yang, Kautz & Hatamizadeh — Gated Delta Networks (ICLR 2025). arXiv:2412.06464. Decay × delta rule; currently the default linear layer. Pair with Yang et al., Parallelizing DeltaNet (arXiv:2406.06484) for the WY-representation kernel that made it practical.
  7. Gu & Dao — Mamba (2023). arXiv:2312.00752. Selectivity and the hardware-aware scan. Read after Mamba-2 if you are short of time — the SSD paper supersedes much of the algorithmic content.
  8. Ren et al. — Samba (ICLR 2025, arXiv:2406.07522) and Lieber et al. — Jamba (arXiv:2403.19887). The hybrid design space and the ablations that justify it.
  9. MiniMax — MiniMax-01: Scaling Foundation Models with Lightning Attention (2025). arXiv:2501.08313. Proof that linear attention scales to frontier size, plus the sliding-window baselines they rejected.
  10. Behrouz, Zhong & Mirrokni — Titans (arXiv:2501.00663) and Sun et al. — Learning to (Learn at Test Time) (arXiv:2407.04620). The "state as an online learner" framing, taken seriously.
  11. Implementations: fla-org/flash-linear-attention is the reference library — Triton kernels for essentially every architecture in this guide, and the fastest way to understand the chunkwise form is to read its code.

ADerivations

A.1 The chunkwise form, derived

Start from the recurrence with decay γ\gamma γ and split the sequence into chunks of size CCC. Let chunk [i][i][i] cover positions iC…iC+C−1iC \ldots iC+C-1iC…iC+C−1, and let S[i]S[i]S[i] be the state entering that chunk.

r=t−iCot=qt⊤St=qt⊤(γr+1S[i]⏟inter-chunk+∑s≤rγr−sksvs⊤⏟intra-chunk)Ointer=(Q[i]⊙γr+1)S[i]Ointra=(Q[i]K[i]⊤⊙M)V[i]Mrs={γr−s,s≤r0,s>rS[i+1]=γCS[i]+(K[i]⊙γC−s)⊤V[i]\begin{aligned}r&=t-iC\\ o_t&=q_t^\top S_t\\ &=q_t^\top\left(\underbrace{\gamma^{r+1}S[i]}_{\text{inter-chunk}}+\underbrace{\sum_{s\le r}\gamma^{r-s}k_sv_s^\top}_{\text{intra-chunk}}\right)\\ O_{\mathrm{inter}}&=(Q[i]\odot\gamma^{r+1})S[i]\\ O_{\mathrm{intra}}&=(Q[i]K[i]^\top\odot M)V[i]\\ M_{rs}&=\begin{cases}\gamma^{r-s},&s\le r\\0,&s>r\end{cases}\\ S[i+1]&=\gamma^CS[i]+(K[i]\odot\gamma^{C-s})^\top V[i]\end{aligned}rot​Ointer​Ointra​Mrs​S[i+1]​=t−iC=qt⊤​St​=qt⊤​​inter-chunkγr+1S[i]​​+intra-chunks≤r∑​γr−sks​vs⊤​​​​=(Q[i]⊙γr+1)S[i]=(Q[i]K[i]⊤⊙M)V[i]={γr−s,0,​s≤rs>r​=γCS[i]+(K[i]⊙γC−s)⊤V[i]​

Four GEMMs and two elementwise masks per chunk. Cost: O(C2d)O(C^{2}d)O(C2d) for the intra term and O(Cd2)O(Cd^{2})O(Cd2) for the inter terms, so per token O(Cd+d2)O(Cd + d^{2})O(Cd+d2). Minimising over CCC alone would give CCC small, but parallelism and SRAM residency push it up — hence the empirical 64–256.

For a data-dependent gate the mask becomes Mrs=∏u=s+1rαuM_{rs} = \prod _{u=s+1}^{r} \alpha _uMrs​=∏u=s+1r​αu​, a cumulative product. Computing it directly underflows, so it is done as a cumulative sum of logs, which is the FP32-only step referred to in §3 and §8.2.

A.2 The delta rule as online gradient descent

Define a per-step objective: the state should map key to value.

Lt(S)=12∥S⊤kt−vt∥2∇SLt=kt(S⊤kt−vt)⊤St=St−1−βt∇SLt=St−1−βtkt(St−1⊤kt−vt)⊤=St−1−βtktkt⊤St−1+βtktvt⊤=(I−βtktkt⊤)St−1+βtktvt⊤\begin{aligned}\mathcal L_t(S)&=\frac12\|S^\top k_t-v_t\|^2\\ \nabla_S\mathcal L_t&=k_t(S^\top k_t-v_t)^\top\\ S_t&=S_{t-1}-\beta_t\nabla_S\mathcal L_t\\ &=S_{t-1}-\beta_tk_t(S_{t-1}^\top k_t-v_t)^\top\\ &=S_{t-1}-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top S_{t-1}+\beta_tk_tv_t^\top\\ &=(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)S_{t-1}+\beta_tk_tv_t^\top\end{aligned}Lt​(S)∇S​Lt​St​​=21​∥S⊤kt​−vt​∥2=kt​(S⊤kt​−vt​)⊤=St−1​−βt​∇S​Lt​=St−1​−βt​kt​(St−1⊤​kt​−vt​)⊤=St−1​−βt​kt​kt⊤​St−1​+βt​kt​vt⊤​=(I−βt​kt​kt⊤​)St−1​+βt​kt​vt⊤​​

Adding weight decay α\alpha α gives the gated form. Reading the correspondence off:

βt: learning rate; binding overwrite strengthαt: decay factor; how fast memory fadesS: associative-memory parameters, fit online1 token⟷1 optimization step\begin{aligned}\beta_t&:\ \text{learning rate; binding overwrite strength}\\ \alpha_t&:\ \text{decay factor; how fast memory fades}\\ S&:\ \text{associative-memory parameters, fit online}\\ 1\text{ token}&\longleftrightarrow1\text{ optimization step}\end{aligned}βt​αt​S1 token​: learning rate; binding overwrite strength: decay factor; how fast memory fades: associative-memory parameters, fit online⟷1 optimization step​

This is why the Test-Time Training / Titans line of work is the same line of work: once the state is "parameters fit by an optimiser," you can swap in momentum, second-order updates, or a deeper memory model, and each choice yields a new architecture.

A.3 Why (I−βkk⊤)(I - \beta kk^\top )(I−βkk⊤) is cheap in chunk form

A chunk applies a product of CCC such matrices to the incoming state:

S[i+1]=(I−βCkCkC⊤)⋯(I−β1k1k1⊤)S[i]+writes\begin{aligned}S[i+1]&=(I-\beta_Ck_Ck_C^\top)\cdots(I-\beta_1k_1k_1^\top)S[i]\\ &\quad+\text{writes}\end{aligned}S[i+1]​=(I−βC​kC​kC⊤​)⋯(I−β1​k1​k1⊤​)S[i]+writes​

Naively that is CCC sequential d×dd\times dd×d updates — exactly the serial dependency chunking exists to avoid. The classical result is that a product of Householder-like rank-1 updates has a compact WY representation:

∏t=1C(I−βtktkt⊤)=I−WT⊤W,T∈Rd×CBuilt from K[i],β using a C×C triangular solve.\begin{aligned}\prod_{t=1}^C(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)&=I-WT^\top\\ W,T&\in\mathbb R^{d\times C}\\ &\text{Built from }K[i],\beta\text{ using a }C\times C\text{ triangular solve.}\end{aligned}t=1∏C​(I−βt​kt​kt⊤​)W,T​=I−WT⊤∈Rd×CBuilt from K[i],β using a C×C triangular solve.​

So the whole chunk's erase operation becomes two GEMMs and one small triangular solve, rather than CCC sequential rank-1 updates. This is the transformation that made DeltaNet trainable at scale, and it is a good illustration of the field's actual bottleneck: the architecture was published in the 1980s; the kernel was published in 2024.

BBackground concepts

The linear algebra, the learning-theory framing and the hardware vocabulary this guide leans on. Skip what you know.

B.1 Linear algebra and numerics

ConceptMeaning, and where it appears here
Outer product kv⊤k v^\top kv⊤A column vector times a row vector, giving a full matrix (as opposed to the inner product k⊤vk^\top vk⊤v, which gives a scalar). Every linear-attention write is an outer product — that is exactly why the state is a matrix rather than a vector. §0.3.
Associativity(AB)C=A(BC)(AB)C = A(BC)(AB)C=A(BC). Trivially true, and it is the entire foundation of the subject: reassociating (ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k))v(\phi (q)^\top \phi (k))v(ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k))v into ϕ(q)⊤(ϕ(k)v⊤)\phi (q)^\top (\phi (k)v^\top )ϕ(q)⊤(ϕ(k)v⊤) turns O(n)O(n)O(n) work per query into O(1)O(1)O(1). The cost of the trick is that softmax's exp⁡(q⊤k)\exp(q^\top k)exp(q⊤k) does not factorise, so you must give it up. §0.2.
Associative memoryA store you address by content rather than by index: write a set of (key, value) bindings, then present a key and get its value back. A matrix S=∑ikivi⊤S=\sum_i k_iv_i^\topS=∑i​ki​vi⊤​ is the simplest one — reading is S⊤kS^\top kS⊤k, and it works because different keys are roughly orthogonal. Interference between non-orthogonal keys is the failure the delta rule fixes. §0.3, §4.
Hopfield networkThe classical (1982) neural associative memory using exactly this outer-product write rule, with well-studied capacity limits. Modern linear attention is a direct descendant, which is why capacity arguments from that literature transfer.
Householder reflectionA matrix of the form I−βkk⊤I - \beta kk^\top I−βkk⊤. Geometrically it reflects (or, for the right β\beta β, projects) away the component of a vector along kkk, leaving everything orthogonal to kkk untouched. Standard equipment in QR factorisation. In §4 it is the "erase this key's old binding" operator.
WY representationA classical numerical-linear-algebra identity: a product of many Householder matrices can be written compactly as I−WT⊤I - W T^\top I−WT⊤ with two thin matrices. This converts a chain of CCC sequential rank-1 updates into two matrix multiplications — which is precisely what made the delta rule trainable at scale. §A.3.
Rank-1 updateAdding an outer product to a matrix. Cheap in arithmetic but sequential: each depends on the last. Turning chains of rank-1 updates into GEMMs is the recurring engineering problem of this field.
Semiseparable matrixA matrix whose every sub-block below the diagonal has low rank. Multiplying by one is equivalent to running a linear recurrence — which is the formal bridge in the SSD duality (§5) between "SSM" and "masked attention." The decay mask Lij=γi−jL_{ij} = \gamma ^{i-j}Lij​=γi−j is the simplest example.
Cumulative product, and log spaceA channel-wise gate needs ∏uαu\prod_u\alpha_u∏u​αu​ over a chunk. Multiplying hundreds of numbers below 1 underflows floating point, so you compute exp⁡(∑ulog⁡αu)\exp(\sum_u\log\alpha_u)exp(∑u​logαu​) instead. The catch: log⁡\loglog/exp⁡\expexp and the sums must be FP32 and cannot run on tensor cores — the constraint that forces GLA's two-level chunking. §3, §8.2.
ELU, SiLU, GroupNormActivation and normalisation primitives. elu⁡(x)+1\operatorname{elu}(x)+1elu(x)+1 is the original feature map ϕ\phi ϕ, chosen because it is strictly positive so the denominator cannot vanish. GroupNorm normalises within groups of channels; RetNet exploits its scale invariance (GroupNorm⁡(α⋅x)=GroupNorm⁡(x)\operatorname{GroupNorm}(\alpha \cdot x) = \operatorname{GroupNorm}(x)GroupNorm(α⋅x)=GroupNorm(x)) to rescale retention scores freely for numerical stability.

B.2 Learning-theory framing

ConceptMeaning, and where it appears
Delta rule / Widrow–HoffThe 1960 learning rule "adjust in proportion to the error": Δw∝(target−prediction)⋅input\Delta w\propto(\mathrm{target}-\mathrm{prediction})\cdot\mathrm{input}Δw∝(target−prediction)⋅input. Applied to an associative memory it says read what is currently stored for this key, then write only the correction — which is precisely §4's update. Equivalent to one step of gradient descent on squared error (§A.2).
Online / stochastic gradient descentUpdating parameters after each example rather than after a full pass. The "state as online learner" view of §4 says a linear-attention layer is running SGD on an associative-memory objective inside the forward pass, one step per token.
Learning rate, weight decay, momentumThe three standard optimiser knobs, and the three roles the gates play under that reading: β\beta β is the learning rate (how hard to overwrite), α\alpha α is weight decay (how fast everything fades), and momentum is what the 2026 variants add. This is why "which optimiser do you want in your forward pass?" is a real architecture question.
Inductive biasThe preferences an architecture brings before seeing data — what it finds easy to represent. Decay is an inductive bias toward recency; the delta rule is one toward clean overwriting.
MQARMulti-Query Associative Recall: a synthetic task presenting many key–value pairs then querying several of them. The standard probe for recall capacity, because performance on it tracks state size almost perfectly. §6.
Pareto frontierThe set of configurations where improving one objective necessarily worsens another. §6's central figure is a Pareto plot of recall against state size: moving along it (more state) is easy, moving it up (better recall per byte) is what a genuinely better write rule achieves.
Big-O, Ω, and why constants winO(f)O(f)O(f) upper-bounds, Ω(f)\Omega (f)Ω(f) lower-bounds. Linear attention is O(n)O(n)O(n) and softmax attention O(n2)O(n^{2})O(n2), yet softmax is faster below ~2K tokens — asymptotics describe the shape of the curve, not where you sit on it. §1.3.
Information-theoretic vs architectural limitsAn architectural limit can be engineered around; an information-theoretic one cannot, because it follows from counting bits. §6's Ω(N)-bits result is the second kind — which is why hybrids (§7) exist rather than better recurrences.
Streaming / small-space modelA computation that reads its input once, in order, keeping only a bounded summary. Linear attention is literally this, which places it in a small-space complexity class and bounds what it can compute regardless of how long you run it.

B.3 Hardware vocabulary

TermMeaning
GEMMGEneral Matrix–Matrix multiply. The operation all accelerators are built around. "Does it reduce to GEMMs?" is the first question to ask of any proposed recurrence (§8.2) — a bespoke sequential scan achieves a fraction of peak where a GEMM achieves most of it.
Tensor coreA matrix multiply–accumulate unit with hardware-specific shapes, input formats, and accumulator precision. FP32 state can coexist with low-precision tensor-core matrix products; supported TF32 or FP64 paths vary by device. Elementwise log-space gates usually use ordinary arithmetic without preventing other parts of the kernel from using tensor cores.
SRAM vs HBMOn-chip scratchpad (tens of MB, ~19 TB/s on H100) versus off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (tens of GB, ~3.35 TB/s). The chunk size CCC is chosen so the working set fits in the first. §8.3.
SM, occupancyStreaming Multiprocessor — the independent compute unit (132 on an H100); occupancy is how many are kept busy. "The non-materialization version lacks sequence-level parallelism" (§1.3) means it can only fill the SMs from batch × heads, which is not enough at long context and small batch.
MaterializationWriting an intermediate to HBM rather than keeping it in SRAM. Storing chunk states lets all chunks be processed in parallel afterwards, at the cost of memory traffic — the central trade in FlashLinearAttention, and the same trade FlashAttention makes between recomputation and storage.
FP32 accumulationMultiplying in low precision but summing in 32-bit. Essential here because the state is a running sum over thousands of outer products; BF16 accumulation drifts. Note the accumulator must persist across the whole chunk loop, not just one tile. §8.3.

CGlossary

Chunkwise parallel formRecurrent across chunks, quadratic within them. The only form that is both parallel and sub-quadratic; the one all fast kernels implement.
Decay / forget gateThe scalar or per-channel factor multiplying the state each step. Fixed (RetNet), data-dependent scalar (Mamba-2), or channel-wise (GLA, KDA).
Delta ruleUpdate that erases a key's existing binding before writing the new one: S←(I−βkk⊤)S+βkv⊤S \leftarrow (I - \beta kk^\top )S + \beta kv^\top S←(I−βkk⊤)S+βkv⊤. Equivalent to one gradient step on ∥S⊤k−v∥2\|S^\top k - v\|^{2}∥S⊤k−v∥2.
Feature map φThe function making similarity factorisable, sim⁡(q,k)=ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k)\operatorname{sim}(q,k) = \phi (q)^\top \phi (k)sim(q,k)=ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k). Must be positive; elu⁡(x)+1\operatorname{elu}(x)+1elu(x)+1 in the original, often learned or a Taylor approximation of exp⁡\expexp since.
Hybrid ratioLinear layers per full-attention layer. 3:1 (Qwen3-Next, Kimi Linear) to 7:1 (MiniMax-01, Jamba).
MaterializationWhether chunk-level states are written to HBM (enabling sequence-level parallelism) or kept in SRAM (saving memory). The central implementation choice in FlashLinearAttention.
MQARMulti-query associative recall — the synthetic task on which the state-size/recall frontier is measured.
SelectivityMamba's term for input-dependent Δ,B,C\Delta , B, CΔ,B,C. The SSM-side name for data-dependent gating.
Semiseparable matrixThe structured matrix class whose multiplication is equivalent to an SSM recurrence; the bridge in the SSD duality.
SSDStructured State-Space Duality — the framework showing SSMs and masked attention are two views of one object, and the matmul-based algorithm that follows.
StateThe dk×dvd_k \times d_vdk​×dv​ matrix per head that replaces the KV cache. Its size is the model's recall capacity (§6).
WY representationCompact factorisation of a product of rank-1 (Householder-like) updates as I−WT⊤I - WT^\top I−WT⊤, turning the delta rule's chunk update into GEMMs.

DCheck yourself

1. What precise memory trade does linear attention make?

It replaces a growing collection of computed KV vectors with a fixed-dimensional recurrent state. At fixed width and precision, memory and update cost do not grow with context length, but the state has a finite information budget. Full attention also uses a learned representation and does not guarantee lossless text storage or perfect retrieval. The formal separation concerns worst-case independent facts that must remain distinguishable, not inevitable failure of every long-distance query. §0, §6.

2. Why is the chunkwise form used everywhere instead of the recurrent form, given the recurrent form has better asymptotics?

Because the recurrent form is fully serial and expresses its work as rank-1 outer products — it cannot use tensor cores and cannot parallelise across the sequence, so it achieves a small fraction of peak. The chunkwise form is recurrent across chunks and quadratic within them, which makes every operation a GEMM. It also subsumes both other forms: C=nC = nC=n is the parallel form, C=1C = 1C=1 the recurrent one. §1.2.

3. Linear attention is O(n)O(n)O(n) and FlashAttention is O(n2)O(n^{2})O(n2). Why is FlashAttention faster below ~2K tokens?

Constants. Linear attention pays O(d2)O(d^{2})O(d2) per token regardless of nnn; softmax attention pays O(n⋅d)O(n\cdot d)O(n⋅d). When n<dn < dn<d, n⋅d<d2n\cdot d < d^{2}n⋅d<d2 and the "efficient" method does more work. Add that FlashAttention is an extremely well-optimised fused kernel and the crossover lands around 2K, with linear attention pulling clearly ahead by 16K. Asymptotics tell you the shape of the curve, not where you are on it. §1.3.

4. Name the two failure modes of plain linear attention and the fix for each.

Never forgets: St=St−1+kv⊤S_{t} = S_{t-1} + kv^\top St​=St−1​+kv⊤ accumulates forever, so the state becomes an average of everything. Fixed by a decay gate α\alpha α — fixed (RetNet), data-dependent (Mamba-2), or channel-wise (GLA). Writes interfere: outer-product writes superimpose, so a new key similar to an old one corrupts the old binding. Fixed by the delta rule, which erases before writing. Gated DeltaNet does both, and beats models that do only one. §2–§4.

5. What does the finite-state recall argument claim, and what does it not claim?

For N independently chosen values from a vocabulary of size V at N known keys, zero-error recall of any requested key requires distinguishing Vᴺ assignments. A b-bit state has at most 2ᵇ possibilities, so b≥Nlog₂V. This is a worst-case zero-error argument under a finite-precision state model. It does not forbid compression of predictable data, approximate recall, preserving selected facts, external memory, or successful finite benchmarks. Hybrid full-attention layers add context-growing storage, but their existence alone does not guarantee that training learns to use it correctly. §6.

6. Why do several deployed model families mix recurrent and full-attention layers?

The full-attention layers preserve context-growing KV storage while recurrent layers reduce average cache and attention costs. The reported examples include 3:1 and 7:1 ratios, but these are architectural and empirical choices, not a theorem that every model must be hybrid or that one ratio always suffices. A 3:1 hybrid retains roughly one quarter of the full KV growth at matched dimensions; long-context memory savings therefore approach 4×, even if an individual recurrent layer saves far more. Retrieval, reasoning, latency, and state precision must be evaluated for each recipe. §7.

7. A colleague proposes a more expressive recurrent update. What execution questions should come first?

Derive both the token recurrence and a chunk implementation, then identify the matrix multiplications, scans, triangular solves, and elementwise gates. A sequential-looking recurrence may admit an associative scan or a triangular chunk solve; do not infer wall time from notation alone. Measure supported precision, numerical stability, state traffic, register/SRAM use, and kernel efficiency. Log-domain gate preparation can use ordinary arithmetic while the large matrix products still use tensor cores. §3, §5, §8.2.

8. When does linear attention improve concurrency more than single-request latency?

At short or moderate context, shared weight reads may dominate single-request latency while per-request KV capacity limits the batch. Replacing those KV entries with smaller recurrent states can then improve capacity more strongly than isolated latency. At very long context, KV reads may dominate latency too. Quantify dimensions and precision: the worked example uses 32 GiB full KV versus 128 MiB FP32 state for a pure recurrent stack, while a 3:1 hybrid retains about one quarter of the KV growth. Neither a universal 500× whole-model saving nor a universal small latency gain follows. §8.1.

9. What working set should you count when sizing SRAM for a recurrent chunk kernel?

Count the state, Q/K/V tiles, intra-chunk scores, and any gates or triangular factors that are live simultaneously. At d=C=128, one 128×128 FP32 state is 64 KiB, three BF16 C×d tiles total 96 KiB, and a BF16 C×C score tile is 32 KiB: already 192 KiB before other buffers. Tiling and reuse may avoid holding all full arrays simultaneously, so this is a transparent example rather than a mandatory allocation. Spilling a fixed-size state raises traffic but does not turn it into a context-growing KV cache. §8.3.

10. Why does a hybrid stack need more than one kernel cost model?

Chunked recurrent training or prefill can exploit matrix products, while recurrent decode may be limited by reading and writing a matrix state. For FP32 state, the simple ungated update/readout has state-only intensity about 0.5 FLOP/byte; scalar gating makes it about 0.625. Full-attention layers add context-growing KV traffic. A hybrid therefore requires separate measurements by phase, state precision, batch, and context, plus support for both recurrent state and paged KV. §8.3.
